questions.prompt: In a meadow food web, an arrow points from grass to a rabbit. What does that arrow represent?

choices.text: Matter and energy moving into the rabbit when it eats the grass
choices.rationale: Correct. The arrowhead lands on the eater. Molecules of grass become part of the rabbit, and the chemical energy stored in them goes along.

choices.text: Energy moving from the rabbit back into the grass
choices.rationale: This reverses the arrow. Energy goes toward the arrowhead, which is the rabbit, not the grass.

choices.text: The rabbit hopping across the meadow toward the grass
choices.rationale: Food-web arrows do not show how animals travel. They show what is passed along when one organism is eaten.

choices.text: Only energy moving to the rabbit while the grass's matter stays behind
choices.rationale: Matter moves too. The grass's carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms end up in the rabbit's body, its breath, or its wastes.

questions.explanation: Food-web arrows point from the food toward the organism that eats it. When the rabbit eats grass, the grass's molecules become rabbit matter, and the chemical energy stored in those molecules travels with them. One arrow stands for both matter and energy moving.
questions.misconception: Food-web arrows show where an animal moves, or only energy moves along them.
questions.hint: Ask what actually ends up inside the rabbit after the meal.

evidence.supports: Arrows in a food web point away from prey and toward the predator because the prey's energy and matter become the predator's energy and matter.

questions.prompt: Over several years, a fallen log on the forest floor rots until almost nothing is left. What happened to the matter that made up the log?

choices.text: Decomposers broke it down into carbon dioxide, water and nutrients
choices.rationale: Correct. The atoms still exist; they moved into the air and soil, where producers can use them again. Some atoms also became part of the fungi and bacteria themselves, and some stay in the soil as dark humus, but none of them vanished.

choices.text: It was destroyed as the wood rotted, so those atoms no longer exist
choices.rationale: Rotting doesn't destroy atoms. Matter changes form and place, but the atoms are conserved.

choices.text: It was turned into energy that the decomposers used up
choices.rationale: Decomposers release the energy stored in the wood's chemical bonds, but the atoms themselves don't become energy; they leave in new molecules.

choices.text: It sank deeper into the ground as the same wood, just out of sight
choices.rationale: The wood doesn't stay as wood; decomposers change it into simpler substances such as carbon dioxide and nutrients.

questions.explanation: Fungi and bacteria feed on the log, and their cellular respiration releases its carbon as carbon dioxide and its other atoms as water and nutrients. Some atoms also became part of the fungi and bacteria themselves, and some stay in the soil as dark humus, but none of them vanished. The matter returns to the air and soil, where plants take it up again.

evidence.supports: The matter that makes up living organisms is conserved and recycled between living things and the environment.

choices.text: It leaves as wastes and as carbon dioxide and water vapor breathed out
choices.rationale: Correct. Only a small part of the grass is built into new body tissue; the rest of its matter leaves in dung and urine and in the carbon dioxide and water vapor the bison breathes out.

choices.rationale: Heat is energy, not a substance. It can't carry atoms away; the atoms leave in dung, urine and breath.

questions.explanation: Matter is conserved, so the grass's mass has to go somewhere. Only a small fraction becomes new bison tissue.

questions.accessiblePrompt: In a simplified model, a young goat eats 2.0 kilograms of food in one day. Of that food, 1.1 kilograms leaves as dung and urine and 0.1 kilograms becomes new body tissue. The rest of the food's matter leaves in carbon dioxide and water vapor from cellular respiration. How many kilograms is that?
questions.conditions: Count only the food's own matter. Ignore any water the goat drinks.
questions.limitations: The numbers are a made-up teaching model. In real respiration, oxygen breathed in also becomes part of the carbon dioxide and water breathed out, so the gas mass breathed out is larger than the food mass it came from. Goats, like cows and bison, also burp out a little methane; this model leaves it out.
questions.workedSolution: Matter is conserved, so every kilogram eaten must be accounted for: 2.0 kg eaten - 1.1 kg dung and urine - 0.1 kg new tissue = 0.8 kg of the food's matter leaving in carbon dioxide and water vapor.
questions.explanation: Because matter is conserved, the food's mass has to show up somewhere: in wastes, in new tissue, or in the carbon dioxide and water released by cellular respiration. Subtracting the known parts from the total gives 0.8 kg leaving through respiration.
questions.misconception: Food that isn't stored as body mass simply disappears.
questions.hint: All 2.0 kg must go somewhere. Subtract the parts you already know.

evidence.supports: Eaten matter partly leaves as waste and partly becomes carbon dioxide during cellular respiration; only a fraction becomes the eater's biomass.

evidence.title: Biology 2e, 46.3 Biogeochemical Cycles
evidence.supports: Matter in living organisms is conserved; respiration returns organic carbon to carbon dioxide.

choices.rationale: Correct. At every step, much of a level is never eaten and goes to decomposers, and eaters release much of their food as wastes and respired carbon dioxide, so little is built into new biomass higher up.

choices.text: Matter is destroyed a little each time one organism eats another

choices.text: Tuna are large, so a few of them need less total food than tiny plankton do

choices.text: Phytoplankton keep making new matter out of sunlight, so the base grows
choices.rationale: Sunlight isn't matter. Phytoplankton build their mass from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight's energy.

questions.explanation: Each level passes on only a fraction of the matter it makes. Many organisms are never eaten, and of the food that is eaten, much leaves as wastes and as carbon dioxide from respiration. The matter isn't gone; it has left the food chain for decomposers and the environment.
questions.misconception: Matter is destroyed or used up as it moves up a food chain.

questions.prompt: Suppose a lake's zooplankton level stores 2,000 kJ of energy per square meter in a year, and the small fish that eat them store 240 kJ per square meter. What percent of the energy stored by the zooplankton ended up stored in the small fish?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Suppose a lake's zooplankton level stores 2,000 kilojoules of energy per square meter in a year, and the small fish that eat them store 240 kilojoules per square meter. What percent of the energy stored by the zooplankton ended up stored in the small fish?
questions.conditions: Example numbers for one lake in one year.
questions.limitations: Real transfer percentages vary between ecosystems and organisms; 10 percent is only an average.
questions.workedSolution: Percent transferred = (energy stored at the higher level ÷ energy stored at the lower level) × 100 = (240 kJ ÷ 2,000 kJ) × 100 = 12%.
questions.explanation: Divide the energy stored by the small fish by the energy stored by the zooplankton and multiply by 100: 240 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 12 percent. That is close to the 10 percent model but not exactly 10, a reminder that the 10 percent rule is an average and real transfers vary.

questions.hint: What fraction of 2,000 is 240? Turn it into a percent.

questions.prompt: To check whether the lake's algae were declining, scientists couldn't count every algal cell in the whole lake. Which method gives the best estimate of the total?
questions.accessiblePrompt: To check whether the lake's algae were declining, scientists couldn't count every algal cell in the whole lake. Which method gives the best estimate of the total?

choices.text: Average cell counts from measured samples at several spots, then scale up
choices.rationale: Correct. Measured samples from several places give a fair average, and scaling up by the lake's volume turns it into a whole-lake estimate.

choices.text: Count the cells in a single drop and report that count as the whole lake's total
choices.rationale: One drop is a tiny sample. Its count must be scaled up by the lake's volume, and one spot may not be typical.

choices.text: Judge from the shore by how green the water looks each week
choices.rationale: Color is a rough clue, but it gives no number and can't be compared fairly from one week to the next.

choices.text: Count cells from the single greenest spot near shore and scale up
choices.rationale: Scaling up is right, but one unusually green spot is not typical and would overestimate the lake; samples must come from several places.

questions.explanation: Scientists estimate huge populations by sampling. Counting cells in measured amounts of water from several places, averaging, and multiplying by the lake's volume gives a number they can compare before and after a change.

questions.prompt: Sewage nutrients made algae grow out of control in the lake, and the water lost much of its dissolved oxygen. Which process uses up large amounts of oxygen when algae overgrow?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Sewage nutrients made algae grow out of control in the lake, and the water lost much of its dissolved oxygen. Which process uses up large amounts of oxygen when algae overgrow?

choices.text: Decomposers using up oxygen as they break down dead algae
choices.rationale: Correct. When masses of algae die and sink, decomposers feeding on them use up dissolved oxygen through cellular respiration.

choices.text: The algae's photosynthesis turns the water's oxygen into sugar
choices.rationale: Photosynthesis releases oxygen; it doesn't turn oxygen into sugar.

choices.text: The sewage nutrients destroy the oxygen atoms in the water
choices.rationale: Atoms aren't destroyed. Oxygen is used up when living things combine it with food during respiration.

choices.text: Fish breathe faster whenever the water turns cloudy
choices.rationale: Cloudy water doesn't make fish breathe faster, and fish use far less oxygen than the decomposers feeding on masses of dead algae.

questions.explanation: Extra nutrients feed an algae boom, but algae don't live forever. When huge numbers die, decomposers feast on them, and their cellular respiration draws down the dissolved oxygen other organisms need. Living algae also use some oxygen in their own respiration, especially at night when they can't photosynthesize, which is the part the textbook mentions, but the biggest drain usually comes from decomposers.
questions.misconception: Algae remove oxygen through photosynthesis, or nutrients destroy oxygen directly.
questions.hint: Oxygen is used up by respiration. Which organisms would suddenly have far more food than usual?

questions.prompt: Use the 10 percent model. The hawks in a grassland store 25 kJ of energy, and they are three feeding steps beyond the producers. How much energy must the producers store to support them?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Use the 10 percent model. The hawks in a grassland store 25 kilojoules of energy, and they are three feeding steps beyond the producers. How much energy must the producers store to support them?
questions.conditions: Use exactly 10 percent per step: each level passes one tenth of its energy to the level that eats it.
questions.limitations: The 10 percent model is an average; real ecosystems transfer more or less than this at each step.
questions.workedSolution: Work back one step at a time, multiplying by 10: 25 kJ × 10 = 250 kJ, then 250 kJ × 10 = 2,500 kJ, then 2,500 kJ × 10 = 25,000 kJ for the producers.
questions.explanation: Each step up keeps only a tenth of the energy, so each step down needs ten times as much. Three steps back from the hawks means multiplying by 10 three times: 25 kJ becomes 25,000 kJ. That is why a few top predators depend on a huge base of producers.
questions.misconception: Working down a pyramid, you multiply by 0.1 again instead of by 10.
questions.hint: Going up, you multiply by 0.10 each step. What should you do at each step going back down?

evidence.locator: Section 4. Energy in Food Webs, Figure 4
evidence.supports: In the 10 percent model, 10,000 units of producer energy are needed to supply 10 units of energy to a top predator three levels up.

evidence.title: Energy Flow and the 10 Percent Rule
evidence.supports: On average about 10 percent of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next.
